Forgotten Roadster: The Unusual 1964 Lightburn “Zeta Sports”

CA
By Chloe Adams Car Culture & Restomod Editor • via Silodrome Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Silodrome Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • This is a 1964 Lightburn Zeta Sports, it’s a pint-sized roadster from Australia powered by a rear-mounted engine that drives the rear wheels through a 4-speed manual transmission.

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • CHLOE ADAMS Car Culture & Restomod Editor

Heritage Preservation vs Modern Performance

Automotive passion is increasingly defined by the synthesis of analog soul and contemporary engineering. This coverage from Silodrome illustrates how bespoke builders, private collectors, and restomod artists are preserving the golden eras of internal combustion while adopting carbon fiber composites and precision craftsmanship.

Big Picture: Auction hammer prices and enthusiast demand indicate sustained historical appreciation for rare, analog driver's vehicles.

This is a 1964 Lightburn Zeta Sports, it’s a pint-sized roadster from Australia powered by a rear-mounted engine that drives the rear wheels through a 4-speed manual transmission.

📌 The Core Development

It’s believed that only 28-50 of these cars were ever made, and they remain largely forgotten today, even in Australia. It’s not known how many have survived, however some estimates put the number in the single digits.

Lightburn & Co was an Adelaide, Australia-based manufacturer of washing machines and cement mixers , so it might seem odd that they seemingly suddenly decided, in the early 1960s, to put their own sports car into production. The company had actually started out as a motor car repair garage that Albert Henry Lightburn opened behind his family home in the Adelaide suburb of Unley in 1919, so the automotive link had always been there.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The Lightburn Zeta Sports had its origins in the Frisky Sprint from England, which Gordon Bedson and his development engineer Keith Peckmore had developed at Henry Meadows Ltd in Wolverhampton. Bedson was a former Vickers aircraft engineer who had designed Stirling Moss’s 500cc Formula 3 car at Kieft. Image courtesy of Lightburn & Co.

Lightburn’s oldest son, Harold, had taken over the company after Albert died in October 1940 and, from 1941, moved it into manufacturing, starting with workshop equipment like Lightning hydraulic jacks. Washing machines followed in 1949, along with concrete mixers, and then fiberglass boats. Because why not.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

The first of Harold Lightburn’s production cars to go on sale was the Zeta Runabout, a fiberglass sedan that launched in 1963 at £595 (about $1,330 USD). A 324cc Villiers two-stroke twin drove the front wheels, and there was no reverse gear – to back up, the driver stopped the engine, then restarted it running backwards, which allowed the regular forward gears to move it in reverse. It was a clever arrangement.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Zeta was the brand Lightburn used for all its cars, so the sedan was sold as the Zeta Runabout, the pickup as the Zeta Utility, and the roadster as the Zeta Sports. The timeline of the various model releases is a little haphazard, the Zeta Sports was developed first, but went on sale after the Zeta Runabout sedan and the Zeta Utility. No one is quite sure why, and the actual reason seems to be lost to history.

The Lightburn Zeta Sports had its origins in the Frisky Sprint from England, which Gordon Bedson and his development engineer Keith Peckmore had developed at Henry Meadows Ltd in Wolverhampton. Bedson was a former Vickers aircraft engineer who had designed Stirling Moss’s 500cc Formula 3 car at Kieft.
